facts.statement: Pteranodon lived during the Late Cretaceous period, specifically from the Santonian to Campanian stages.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Late Cretaceous (Santonian-Campanian),

facts.statement: Pteranodon inhabited North America during the Late Cretaceous, with fossils found in present-day Kansas, Nebraska, Wyoming, South Dakota, and Alabama.
facts.quote: They lived during the late Cretaceous geological period of North America in present-day Kansas, Nebraska, Wyoming, South Dakota and Alabama.

facts.statement: Approximately 1,200 specimens of Pteranodon are known to science, more than any other pterosaur, many featuring well-preserved skulls and articulated skeletons.
facts.quote: More fossil specimens of Pteranodon have been found than any other pterosaur, with about 1,200 specimens known to science, many of them well preserved with nearly complete skulls and articulated skeletons.

facts.statement: Pteranodon was the first pterosaur species discovered outside of Europe.
facts.quote: Pteranodon was the first pterosaur found outside of Europe.

facts.statement: Othniel Charles Marsh first discovered Pteranodon fossils in 1870 or 1871 within the Late Cretaceous Smoky Hill Chalk deposits of western Kansas.
facts.quote: Its fossils first were found by Othniel Charles Marsh in either 1870 or 1871, in the Late Cretaceous Smoky Hill Chalk deposits of western Kansas.

facts.statement: The initial specimens found by Marsh included partial wing bones and a tooth from the fish Xiphactinus, which Marsh incorrectly assumed belonged to the pterosaur, as all previously known pterosaurs possessed teeth.
facts.quote: These first specimens, YPM 1160 and YPM 1161, consisted of partial wing bones, as well as a tooth from the prehistoric fish Xiphactinus, which Marsh mistakenly believed to belong to this new pterosaur (all known pterosaurs up to that point had teeth).

facts.statement: In 1871, Marsh initially named the discovery Pterodactylus oweni, placing it within the European genus Pterodactylus.
facts.quote: In 1871, Marsh named the find Pterodactylus oweni, assigning it to the well-known (but much smaller) European genus Pterodactylus.

facts.statement: After realizing his name was already taken, Marsh renamed the species Pterodactylus occidentalis in 1872, a name meaning "Western wing finger."
facts.quote: Realizing that the name he had chosen had already been used for Harry Seeley's European pterosaur species Pterodactylus oweni in 1864, Marsh renamed his giant North American pterosaur Pterodactylus occidentalis, meaning "Western wing finger," in his 1872 description of the new specimen.

facts.statement: Edward Drinker Cope named two species, Ornithochirus umbrosus and Ornithochirus harpyia, attempting to assign them to the genus Ornithocheirus, though he misspelled the name by omitting the letter 'e'.
facts.quote: Meanwhile, Marsh's rival Edward Drinker Cope had unearthed several specimens of the large North American pterosaur. Based on these specimens, Cope named two new species, Ornithochirus umbrosus and Ornithochirus harpyia, in an attempt to assign them to the large European genus Ornithocheirus, though he misspelled the name (forgetting the 'e').

facts.statement: Cope published his naming paper in 1872, five days after Marsh, leading to a priority dispute over which names applied to the same species.
facts.quote: Cope's paper naming his species was published in 1872, just five days after Marsh's paper. This resulted in a dispute, fought in the published literature, over whose names had priority in what obviously were the same species.

facts.statement: Cope conceded in 1875 that Marsh's names had priority but argued that Pterodactylus umbrosus represented a distinct species from those named by Marsh.
facts.quote: Cope conceded in 1875 that Marsh's names did have priority over his, but maintained that Pterodactylus umbrosus was a distinct species (but not genus) from any that Marsh had named previously.

facts.statement: The first Pteranodon skull was discovered on May 2, 1876, by Samuel Wendell Williston along the Smoky Hill River in Kansas.
facts.quote: the first Pteranodon skull was found on May 2, 1876, along the Smoky Hill River in Wallace County (now Logan County), Kansas, USA, by Samuel Wendell Williston, a fossil collector working for Marsh.

facts.statement: Marsh described Pteranodon as distinguished from all previously known pterosaur genera by the complete absence of teeth.
facts.quote: Marsh recognized this major difference, describing the specimens as "distinguished from all previously known genera of the order Pterosauria by the entire absence of teeth."

facts.statement: Marsh coined the name Pteranodon, meaning "wing without tooth," in 1876 to establish a new genus for these toothless pterosaurs.
facts.quote: Marsh recognized that this characteristic warranted a new genus, and he coined the name Pteranodon ("wing without tooth") in 1876.

facts.statement: Initially, Pteranodon fossils were assigned to toothed pterosaur genera such as Ornithocheirus and Pterodactylus.
facts.quote: When the first fossils of Pteranodon were found, they were assigned to toothed pterosaur genera, which includes Ornithocheirus and Pterodactylus.

facts.statement: Pteranodon belongs to the family Pteranodontidae and the clade Pteranodontia, which also includes nyctosaurids.
facts.quote: Pteranodon is part of the family Pteranodontidae, part of the clade Pteranodontia, which also includes nyctosaurids.

facts.statement: Pteranodontians form the clade Pteranodontoidea alongside ornithocheiromorphs, which falls under the suborder Pterodactyloidea.
facts.quote: Pteranodontians form a larger clade, Pteranodontoidea, alongside ornithocheiromorphs, and that clade falls under the suborder Pterodactyloidea.

facts.statement: Although not dinosaurs, Pteranodon is part of the clade Avemetatarsalia, making it closely related to dinosaurs.
facts.quote: While not dinosaurs, pterosaurs such as Pteranodon form a clade closely related to dinosaurs as both fall within the clade Avemetatarsalia.

facts.statement: Two distinct morphs of Pteranodon have been identified, representing males and females that differed in size and crest shape.
facts.quote: Two distinct morphs of Pteranodon specimen have been found, that are thought to represent males and females. Male and female Pteranodon differed in size and crest shape.

facts.statement: Male Pteranodon reached wingspans of 5.6 to 7.6 meters, while females were smaller, averaging 3.8 meters.
facts.quote: Males attained wingspans of 5.6 - 7.6 m; females were smaller, averaging 3.8 m.

facts.statement: Female Pteranodon possessed wider pelvises than males.
facts.quote: Females also had wider pelvises than males.

facts.statement: Today, only two species of Pteranodon are recognized: P. longiceps, the type species, and P. sternbergi.
facts.quote: Over the decades, multiple species would be assigned to Pteranodon, though today, only two are recognised: P. longiceps, the type species, and P. sternbergi.

facts.statement: The existence of P. maiseyi is uncertain, and some researchers debate whether P. sternbergi and P. maiseyi should be classified as the separate genus Geosternbergia.
facts.quote: A third species, P. maiseyi, may also exist. Some researchers have suggested the latter two as a genus of their own, Geosternbergia, though this is the subject of some debate.

facts.statement: The relationship between Dawndraco, Geosternbergia, and Pteranodon remains debated, with Dawndraco potentially being synonymous with either Geosternbergia or Pteranodon depending on the validity of the latter genus.
facts.quote: Another genus split from Pteranodon, Dawndraco, may be synonymous with Geosternbergia if that genus is valid, or with Pteranodon if it is not.

facts.statement: Pteranodon was a significant component of the animal community in the Western Interior Seaway.
facts.quote: It was an important part of the animal community in the Western Interior Seaway.

facts.statement: In 1876, Marsh recognized Pteranodon as a unique genus because it completely lacked teeth, a trait not seen in other pterosaurs at that time.
facts.quote: In 1876, Othniel Charles Marsh recognised it as a genus of its own, making particular note of its complete lack of teeth, which at the time was unique among pterosaurs.

facts.statement: S. W. Williston was the first scientist to critically evaluate all Pteranodon species previously classified by Cope and Marsh.
facts.quote: Williston was also the first scientist to critically evaluate all of the Pteranodon species classified by Cope and Marsh.

facts.statement: In 1903, Williston revised the number of valid Pteranodon species from seven down to three.
facts.quote: In 1903, Williston revisited the question of Pteranodon classification, and revised his earlier conclusion that there were seven species down to just three.

facts.statement: In 1910, Eaton published the first detailed description of the entire Pteranodon skeleton known at that time.
facts.quote: In 1910, Eaton became the first scientist to publish a more detailed description of the entire Pteranodon skeleton, as it was known at the time.

facts.statement: Eaton used clay models of bones to test how fossilization pressure affected the shapes of arm bones used in previous classifications.
facts.quote: Eaton conducted experiments using clay models of bones to help determine the effects of crushing and flattening on the shapes of the arm bones Williston had used in his own classification.

facts.statement: Harksen classified specimens with upright crests as the new species Pteranodon sternbergi in 1966.
facts.quote: The discovery of specimens with upright crests, classified by Harksen in 1966 as the new species Pteranodon sternbergi, complicated the situation even further.

facts.statement: Robert Milton Schoch published a revision in 1984 that treated P. longiceps as a synonym of P. ingens.
facts.quote: In 1984, Robert Milton Schoch published another revision that essentially returned to Marsh's original classification scheme, most notably sinking P. longiceps as a synonym of P. ingens.

facts.statement: S. Christopher Bennett published a paper in 1992 discussing sexual dimorphism in Pteranodon, following a similar paper from 1987.
facts.quote: In 1992, he published a paper discussing sexual dimorphism and its role in individual variation among Pteranodon fossils, a follow-up of a 1987 paper he authored on the same subject.

facts.statement: Adult male Pteranodon were the largest known flying animals until the late 20th century.
facts.quote: Adult male Pteranodon were among the largest pterosaurs, and were the largest flying animals known until the late 20th century, when the giant azhdarchid pterosaurs were discovered.

facts.statement: The average adult male Pteranodon had a wingspan of 5.6 meters.
facts.quote: The wingspan of an average adult male Pteranodon was 5.6 m.

facts.statement: Adult female Pteranodon averaged a wingspan of 3.8 meters.
facts.quote: Adult females were much smaller, averaging 3.8 m in wingspan.

facts.statement: A large male specimen (USNM 50130) had an estimated wingspan of 6.25 to 6.5 meters, a body length of 2.6 meters, and a mass of 50 kg.
facts.quote: A large specimen of Pteranodon longiceps, USNM 50130, is estimated to have a wingspan of 6.25 - 6.5 m, body length of 2.6 m and body mass of 50 kg.

facts.statement: The largest known Pteranodon specimens had wingspans ranging from 7.25 to 7.6 meters.
facts.quote: Even larger specimens had wingspans of 7.25 - 7.6 m.

facts.statement: Females had short, rounded crests and wide pelvic canals, while males had narrow hips and large crests likely used for display.
facts.quote: Size aside, females were distinguished by their short, rounded head crests and wide pelvic canals, whereas males had narrow hips and very large head crests, likely serving a display function.

facts.statement: Methods for estimating the mass of large male Pteranodon (wingspans around 7 meters) have been notoriously unreliable.
facts.quote: Methods used to estimate the mass of large male Pteranodon specimens (those with wingspans of about 7 meters) have been notoriously unreliable, producing a wide range of estimates.

facts.statement: A 2010 review by Witton and Habib argued that the maximum mass of Pteranodon is likely between 20 and 35 kg, rather than 93 kg.
facts.quote: In a review of pterosaur size estimates published in 2010, Mark Witton and Michael Habib argued that the largest estimate of 93 kg is much too high and an upper limit of 20–35 kg is more realistic.

facts.statement: Unlike earlier pterosaurs, Pteranodon possessed toothless beaks similar to those of birds.
facts.quote: Unlike earlier pterosaurs, such as Rhamphorhynchus and Pterodactylus, Pteranodon had toothless beaks, similar to those of birds.

facts.statement: The upper jaw was longer than the lower and curved upward, though one specimen shows curvature suggesting the beak widened toward the tip.
facts.quote: The upper jaw, which was longer than the lower jaw, was curved upward; while this normally has been attributed only to the upward-curving beak, one specimen (UALVP 24238) has a curvature corresponding with the beak widening towards the tip.

facts.statement: Alexander Kellner assigned a specimen with a unique beak form to the distinct genus Dawndraco in 2010.
facts.quote: The unique form of the beak in this specimen led Alexander Kellner to assign it to a distinct genus, Dawndraco, in 2010.

facts.statement: The most distinctive feature of Pteranodon is its cranial crest, made of skull bones projecting upward and backward.
facts.quote: The most distinctive characteristic of Pteranodon is its cranial crest. These crests consisted of skull bones (frontals) projecting upward and backward from the skull.

facts.statement: The size and shape of Pteranodon crests varied based on age, sex, and species.
facts.quote: The size and shape of these crests varied due to a number of factors, including age, sex, and species.

facts.statement: Males of the older species P. sternbergi had vertical crests with broad forward projections, while P. longiceps evolved narrower, backward-projecting crests.
facts.quote: Male Pteranodon sternbergi, the older species of the two described to date, had a more vertical crest with a broad forward projection, while their descendants, Pteranodon longiceps, evolved a narrower, more backward-projecting crest.

facts.statement: The neural spines of Pteranodon's vertebrae were narrow.
facts.quote: The neural spines of Pteranodon's vertebrae were narrow.

facts.statement: Pteranodon possessed a notarium, a fused mass of the first six dorsal vertebrae.
facts.quote: Like many pterosaurs and birds, it possessed a notarium, a fused mass comprising the first six dorsal vertebrae.

facts.statement: The scapulae were oriented to brace each other via fusion with the coracoids, increasing structural integrity during flight.
facts.quote: Pteranodon's scapulae were oriented in such a way that each one braces the other, due to their fusion with the coracoids, providing increased integrity during flight.

facts.statement: The first three metacarpals were very slender, with digits sporting short, curved claws.
facts.quote: The first three metacarpals were very slender, and their respective digits sported short, curved unguals (claws).

facts.statement: The hind feet had four metatarsals tipped with less curved claws.
facts.quote: Pteranodon's hind feet had four metatarsals, which were tipped with less curved claws.

facts.statement: Pteranodon likely flew with a flight pattern similar to that of a modern albatross.
facts.quote: The wing shape of Pteranodon suggests that it would have flown rather like a modern-day albatross.

facts.statement: Pteranodon had a high aspect ratio of 9:1, which is similar to the 8:1 ratio found in albatrosses.
facts.quote: This is based on the fact that Pteranodon had a high aspect ratio (wingspan to chord length) similar to that of the albatross — 9:1 for Pteranodon, compared to 8:1 for an albatross.

facts.statement: Pteranodon likely took off from the ground using a standing, quadrupedal position.
facts.quote: Like other pterosaurs, Pteranodon probably took off from a standing, quadrupedal position.

facts.statement: Pteranodon used its long forelimbs to vault itself into the air during takeoff.
facts.quote: Using their long forelimbs for leverage, they would have vaulted themselves into the air in a rapid leap.

facts.statement: Trackway evidence suggests that Pteranodon moved on land as a quadruped.
facts.quote: Trackways suggest that pterosaurs like Pteranodon were quadrupedal.

facts.statement: Fossilized fish bones found in the stomach area and a fish bolus found between the jaws of specimen AMNH 5098 confirm that fish were part of Pteranodon's diet.
facts.quote: fossilized fish bones have been found in the stomach area of one Pteranodon, and a fossilized fish bolus has been found between the jaws of another Pteranodon, specimen AMNH 5098.

facts.statement: Fragments of fish scales and vertebrae found near the torso indicate that fish made up the majority of Pteranodon's diet, though it may have also eaten invertebrates.
facts.quote: Numerous other specimens also preserve fragments of fish scales and vertebrae near the torso, indicating that fish made up a majority of the diet of Pteranodon (though they may also have taken invertebrates).

facts.statement: In 1994, Bennett suggested that Pteranodon could dive by folding back its wings like a modern gannet, based on its heavily built head, neck, and shoulders.
facts.quote: In 1994, Bennett noted that the head, neck, and shoulders of Pteranodon were as heavily built as diving birds, and suggested that they could dive by folding back their wings like the modern gannet.

facts.statement: The function of Pteranodon's skull crest remains a subject of scientific debate.
facts.quote: Pteranodon was notable for its skull crest, though the function of this crest has been a subject of debate.

facts.statement: Many explanations for the crest's function focus on the backward-pointing crest of male P. longiceps while ignoring the wide variation seen across age and sex.
facts.quote: Most explanations have focused on the blade-like, backward pointed crest of male P. longiceps, however, and ignored the wide range of variation across age and sex.

facts.statement: Research suggests that sexual display was the primary function of the crest, with other functions being secondary.
facts.quote: Therefore, display was probably the main function of the crest, and any other functions were secondary.

facts.statement: In 1910, George Francis Eaton proposed that the crest served as an aerodynamic counterbalance or a muscle attachment point.
facts.quote: Scientific interpretations of the crest's function began in 1910, when George Francis Eaton proposed two possibilities: an aerodynamic counterbalance and a muscle attachment point.

facts.statement: In 1943, Dominik von Kripp suggested the crest acted as a rudder, a hypothesis supported by several later researchers.
facts.quote: In 1943, Dominik von Kripp suggested that the crest may have served as a rudder, an idea embraced by several later researchers.

facts.statement: Fossil specimens show that females and juveniles had small crests while males had large, elaborate, and variable crests.
facts.quote: This is consistent with the size variation seen in fossil specimens, where females and juveniles have small crests and males large, elaborate, variable crests.

facts.statement: Large Pteranodon skulls feature large crests pointing upward and backward, whereas small skulls have small, triangular crests.
facts.quote: Skulls from the larger size class preserve large, upward and backward pointing crests, while the crests of the smaller size class are small and triangular.

facts.statement: Some large Pteranodon skulls possess a second low crest extending toward the beak tip, a feature absent in small skulls.
facts.quote: Some larger skulls also show evidence of a second crest that extended long and low, toward the tip of the beak, which is not seen in smaller specimens.

facts.statement: Researchers identified the sex of Pteranodon size classes by examining pelvic bones rather than skulls.
facts.quote: The gender of the different size classes was determined, not from the skulls, but from the pelvic bones.

facts.statement: The smaller Pteranodon size class had unusually large and wide-set pelvic bones, contrary to typical expectations.
facts.quote: Contrary to what may be expected, the smaller size class had disproportionately large and wide-set pelvic bones.

facts.statement: Christopher Bennett interpreted the large pelvic bones of small Pteranodon as evidence of a spacious birth canal for passing eggs.
facts.quote: Bennett interpreted this as indicating a more spacious birth canal, through which eggs would pass.

facts.statement: Bennett concluded that small, triangular-crested Pteranodon were females and large, large-crested ones were males.
facts.quote: He concluded that the small size class with small, triangular crests represent females, and the larger, large-crested specimens represent males.

facts.statement: A 1993 study found subadult Pteranodon had fibrolamellar bone, indicating rapid growth.
facts.quote: A 1993 study by Bennett found that the limb bone shafts of subadult Pteranodon were fibrolamellar bone, which is highly vascularized and characteristic of rapidly growing animals.

facts.statement: In 2017, Bennett described FHSM 17956, the smallest known Pteranodon specimen, as an incomplete right wing from the Smoky Hill Chalk.
facts.quote: In 2017, Bennett described the smallest known specimen of Pteranodon: FHSM 17956, an incomplete right wing from the Smoky Hill Chalk.

facts.statement: Bennett interpreted the juvenile Pteranodon wing found in the open-ocean Smoky Hill Chalk as evidence that juveniles were precocial and capable of long-distance flight.
facts.quote: Bennett interpreted its presence in the Smoky Hill Chalk—an open ocean setting lacking small terrestrial vertebrates—as indication that juvenile Pteranodon were precocial and already capable of flying long distances.

facts.statement: A 2023 study by Yang et al. compared Pteranodon wing growth and performance to Sinopterus, Pterodactylus, Rhamphorhynchus, and anurognathids.
facts.quote: A 2023 study by Yang et al. assessed wing ontogeny and performance in Pteranodon compared to Sinopterus, Pterodactylus, Rhamphorhynchus, and anurognathids.

facts.statement: Pteranodon fossils are found in the Smoky Hill Chalk of the Niobrara Formation and the Sharon Springs deposits of the Pierre Shale Formation.
facts.quote: Specimens assigned to Pteranodon have been found in both the Smoky Hill Chalk deposits of the Niobrara Formation, and the slightly younger Sharon Springs deposits of the Pierre Shale Formation.

facts.statement: Pteranodon lived in an area covered by the Western Interior Seaway, a large inland sea.
facts.quote: When Pteranodon was alive, this area was covered by a large inland sea, known as the Western Interior Seaway.

facts.statement: Evidence suggests Pteranodon's range was limited to the southern Niobrara Formation and did not extend north of South Dakota.
facts.quote: This strongly suggests that the natural geographic range of Pteranodon covered only the southern part of the Niobrara, and that its habitat did not extend farther north than South Dakota.

facts.statement: Pteranodon likely nested on offshore rookeries hundreds of kilometers from the coast to avoid predators and access food.
facts.quote: It is likely that, as in other polygynous animals (in which males compete for association with harems of females), Pteranodon lived primarily on offshore rookeries, where they could nest away from land-based predators and feed far from shore; most Pteranodon fossils are found in locations which at the time, were hundreds of kilometres from the coastline.

facts.statement: Pteranodon fossils are primarily known from the Niobrara Formation in the central United States.
facts.quote: Pteranodon fossils are known primarily from the Niobrara Formation of the central United States.

facts.statement: Kenneth Carpenter's 2003 survey showed P. sternbergi lived from 88 to 85 million years ago, and P. longiceps from 86 to 84.5 million years ago.
facts.quote: in 2003, Kenneth Carpenter surveyed the distribution and dating of fossils in this formation, demonstrating that Pteranodon sternbergi existed there from 88 to 85 million years ago, while P. longiceps existed between 86 and 84.5 million years ago.

facts.statement: Kellner named Geosternbergia maiseyi in 2010 from fossils dating between 81.5 and 80.5 million years ago.
facts.quote: A possible third species, which Kellner named Geosternbergia maiseyi in 2010, is known from the Sharon Springs member of the Pierre Shale Formation in Kansas, Wyoming, and South Dakota, dating to between 81.5 and 80.5 million years ago.

facts.statement: Researchers previously thought the two size classes were different species, but Christopher Bennett argued they represent sexually dimorphic males and females.
facts.quote: while researchers had previously suggested that they represent different species, Christopher Bennett showed that the differences between them are consistent with the concept that they represent females and males, and that Pteranodon species were sexually dimorphic.

facts.statement: Bennett suggested in the early 1990s that the two Pteranodon morphs represent chronospecies within a single lineage due to their temporal separation and similarity.
facts.quote: In the early 1990s, Bennett noted that the two major morphs of pteranodont present in the Niobrara Formation were precisely separated in time with little, if any, overlap. Due to this, and to their gross overall similarity, he suggested that they probably represent chronospecies within a single evolutionary lineage lasting about 4 million years.

facts.statement: The bodies and wings of all Pteranodon specimens were essentially identical, showing little variation in their post-cranial skeletons.
facts.quote: the post-cranial skeletons of Pteranodon show little to no variation between species or specimens

facts.statement: Pteranodon sternbergi is the only known species of Pteranodon that possesses an upright crest.
facts.quote: Pteranodon sternbergi is the only known species of Pteranodon with an upright crest

facts.statement: The lower jaw of Pteranodon sternbergi measured 1.25 meters in length.
facts.quote: The lower jaw of P. sternbergi was 1.25 m long

facts.statement: Pteranodon sternbergi was collected by George F. Sternberg in 1952 and formally described by John Christian Harksen in 1966.
facts.quote: It was collected by George F. Sternberg in 1952 and described by John Christian Harksen in 1966

facts.statement: Pteranodon sternbergi fossils were found in the lower portion of the Niobrara Formation.
facts.quote: from the lower portion of the Niobrara Formation

facts.statement: In 1972, Halsey Wilkinson Miller proposed that different forms of Pteranodon should be classified into distinct subgenera.
facts.quote: In 1972, Halsey Wilkinson Miller published a paper arguing that the various forms of Pteranodon were different enough to be placed in distinct subgenera

facts.statement: In 2010, Alexander Kellner revisited Halsey Wilkinson Miller's classification and argued that Pteranodon species differences warranted placement in different genera.
facts.quote: In 2010, pterosaur researcher Alexander Kellner revisited H.W. Miller's classification

facts.statement: A 2024 phylogenetic analysis reclassified species previously assigned to Geosternbergia back into the genus Pteranodon.
facts.quote: However, both species previously referred to Geosternbergia were separately included as those of Pteranodon (P. sternbergi and P. maiseyi) based on phylogenetic analysis in 2024

facts.statement: Many species of Pteranodon named since the 1870s are now considered junior synonyms of just two or three valid species.
facts.quote: A number of additional species of Pteranodon have been named since the 1870s, although most now are considered to be junior synonyms of two or three valid species

facts.quote: Other valid species include the possibly larger P. sternbergi, with a wingspan originally estimated at 9 m

facts.quote: El grupo de mayor tamaño representaría individuos machos, con caderas estrechas y enormes crestas en su cabeza, la cual era probablemente para despliegues visuales

facts.statement: The average wingspan of an adult male Pteranodon was 5.6 meters.
facts.quote: La envergadura de un macho adulto promedio de Pteranodon era de 5.6 metros

facts.statement: Adult females were much smaller, averaging a wingspan of 3.8 meters.
facts.quote: Las hembras adultas eran mucho menores, promediando los 3.8 metros de envergadura

facts.statement: The largest known Pteranodon longiceps from the Niobrara Formation had a wingspan of 6.25 meters.
facts.quote: El mayor ejemplar de Pteranodon longiceps de la formación Niobrara medía 6.25 metros de la punta de un ala a la otra

facts.statement: A larger specimen with a 7.25-meter wingspan is known from the Pierre Shale Formation.
facts.quote: Un ejemplar aún mayor es conocido de la formación Pierre Shale, con una envergadura de 7.25 metros

facts.statement: A specimen with a 7.25-meter wingspan from the Pierre Shale may actually belong to the distinct species Geosternbergia maysei.
facts.quote: Un ejemplar aún mayor es conocido de la formación Pierre Shale, con una envergadura de 7.25 metros, si bien este espécimen puede pertenecer al género y especie distintos Geosternbergia maysei

facts.statement: Weight estimates for large male Pteranodon (with ~7-meter wingspans) have been unreliable, ranging from as low as 20 kg to as high as 93 kg.
facts.quote: Los métodos usados para estimar el peso de los grandes machos de Pteranodon (aquellos con envergaduras de cerca de 7 metros) han sido notoriamente poco fiables, produciendo una amplia gama de estimaciones desde tan bajas como 20 kg. a tan altas como 93 kg.

facts.statement: Researchers Witton and Habib argued that methods used to produce lower weight estimates were equally deficient.
facts.quote: Witton y Habib consideraron que los métodos usados por otros científicos quienes obtuvieron estimados de peso menores eran igualmente deficientes

facts.statement: Pteranodon possessed a toothless beak similar to that of modern birds, unlike more primitive pterosaurs.
facts.quote: A diferencia de pterosaurios más primitivos como Rhamphorhynchus y Pterodactylus, Pteranodon tenía un pico desdentado, similar al de las aves modernas.

facts.statement: The beak of Pteranodon was composed of solid bony ridges projecting from the base of the jaws.
facts.quote: El pico de Pteranodon estaba hecho de bordes óseos sólidos que se proyectaban desde la base de las mandíbulas.

facts.statement: The upper jaw of Pteranodon was longer than the lower jaw.
facts.quote: La mandíbula superior era más larga que la inferior.

facts.statement: The most distinctive feature of Pteranodon was its cranial crest.
facts.quote: La característica más distintiva de Pteranodon es su cresta craneal.

facts.statement: The cranial crests were projections of the frontal bones extending upwards and backwards from the skull.
facts.quote: Estas crestas eran una proyección de los huesos frontales que se proyectaban hacia arriba y atrás del cráneo.

facts.statement: Females of both species had smaller, rounded crests.
facts.quote: Las hembras de ambas especies tenían crestas más pequeñas y redondeadas.

facts.statement: These crests were likely display structures, though they may have had other functions.
facts.quote: Estas crestas eran probablemente estructuras de exhibición, aunque pudieron haber tenido también otras funciones.

facts.statement: Distinctive features separating Pteranodon from other pterosaurs included narrow neural spines on vertebrae, ligament-like bony plates strengthening vertebrae over the hip, and a relatively short tail with fused vertebrae forming a long bony rod.
facts.quote: Otras características distintivas que apartan a Pteranodon de otros pterosaurios incluyen estrechas espinas neurales en las vértebras, ligamentos similares a placas óseas que fortalecían las vértebras sobre la cadera, y una cola relativamente corta en la cual las últimas vértebras estaban fusionadas en una especie de larga vara ósea.

facts.statement: The total tail length was about 3.5% of the wingspan, or more than 25 centimeters in the largest males.
facts.quote: La longitud entera de la cola era cerca del 3.5% de la envergadura alar, es decir más de 25 centímetros en los mayores machos.

facts.statement: Pteranodon existed for over four million years, from the late Coniacian to the early Campanian of the Cretaceous period.
facts.quote: En sentido amplio, Pteranodon existió por más de cuatro millones de años, desde finales del Coniaciense hasta principios del Campaniense en el período Cretácico.

facts.statement: Pteranodon sternbergi lived between 88 and 85 million years ago, while P. longiceps lived between 86 and 84.5 million years ago.
facts.quote: Pteranodon sternbergi existió entre hace 88 a 85 millones de años, mientras que P. longiceps existió entre hace 86-84.5 millones de años.

facts.statement: A possible third species, named Geosternbergia maysei by Kellner in 2010, is known from the Sharon Springs Member of the Pierre Shale Formation in Kansas, Wyoming, and South Dakota, dating from 81.5 to 80.5 million years ago.
facts.quote: Una posible tercera especie, la cual Kellner llamó Geosternbergia maysei en 2010, es conocida del Miembro Sharon Springs de la formación Pierre Shale en Kansas, Wyoming y Dakota del Sur, datando de entre 81.5 a 80.5 millones de años.

facts.statement: Bennett noted that the two major pteranodont species in the Niobrara Formation were separated precisely in time with little to no overlap.
facts.quote: Bennett notó que las dos especies mayores de pteranodontes presentes en la formación Niobrara estaban separadas precisamente en el tiempo con poca superposición, si la había.

facts.statement: Bennett suggested that the two species likely represented a chronospecies within a single evolutionary lineage lasting about 4 million years.
facts.quote: Debido a esto, y a su similitud general, él sugirió que probablemente representaban una cronoespecie dentro de un único linaje evolutivo que perduró unos 4 millones de años.

facts.statement: When Pteranodon lived, the area was covered by a large inland sea known as the Niobrara Sea.
facts.quote: Cuando Pteranodon vivía, esta área estaba cubierta por un gran mar interior, conocido como el Mar de Niobrara.

facts.statement: Despite numerous fossils found in contemporary parts of the formation in Canada, no pterosaur specimens have been found there.
facts.quote: A pesar del hecho de que numerosos fósiles se han hallado en partes contemporáneas de la formación en Canadá, no se han encontrado ejemplares de pterosaurios allí.

facts.statement: This strongly suggests that the natural geographic range of Pteranodon covered only the southern part of the Niobrara Sea, and its habitat did not extend north of South Dakota.
facts.quote: Esto sugiere fuertemente que el rango geográfico natural de Pteranodon cubría solo la parte sur del mar de Niobrara, y que su hábitat no se extendía más al norte que Dakota del Sur.

facts.statement: Some very fragmentary fossils belonging to pteranodont pterosaurs, and possibly Pteranodon itself, have also been found on the Gulf Coast and East Coast of the United States.
facts.quote: Algunos fósiles muy fragmentarios que pertenecen a pterosaurios pteranodontes, y posiblemente al propio Pteranodon, también se han hallado en la costa del Golfo y en la Costa Este de Estados Unidos.

facts.statement: Some remains from Japan have been tentatively attributed to Pteranodon, but their distance from the Niobrara Sea habitat makes that identification unlikely.
facts.quote: Algunos restos de Japón se han atribuido tentativamente a Pteranodon, pero su distancia del hábitat del mar de Niobrara hace que esa identificación sea improbable.

facts.statement: It is known that at least some of these marine reptiles fed on Pteranodon.
facts.quote: Se sabe que al menos alguno de estos reptiles marinos se alimentaba de Pteranodon.

facts.statement: In 1904, Barnum Brown reported that the stomach area of a plesiosaur contained bones of a "pterodactyl," very likely Pteranodon.
facts.quote: Barnum Brown, en 1904, reportó que el contenido del área del estómago de un plesiosaurio contenía huesos de un "pterodáctilo", muy probablemente de Pteranodon.

facts.statement: The wing shape of Pteranodon suggests it may have flown similarly to a modern albatross.
facts.quote: La forma del ala de Pteranodon sugiere puede haber volado de forma similar a un albatros actual.

facts.statement: This is based on the fact that Pteranodon had a high aspect ratio (wingspan to chord length) similar to an albatross—9:1 for Pteranodon compared to 8:1 for an albatross.
facts.quote: Esto se basa en el hecho de que Pteranodon tenía una alta relación de aspecto (la envergadura en relación con la longitud de la cuerda) similar a la del albatros — 9:1 para Pteranodon, comparada a 8:1 para un albatros.

facts.statement: While much of Pteranodon's flight may have depended on soaring, it likely required occasional bursts of rapid active flapping, and studies of its wing loading indicate it was capable of considerable active flight, contrary to initial ideas that its wings were so large they could only soar.
facts.quote: Aunque mucho del vuelo de un Pteranodon pudo haber dependido del planeo, como las aves marinas de largas alas, probablemente requería de un ocasional estallido activo de aleteo rápido, y estudios de la carga alar de Pteranodon (la fuerza de las alas vs. el peso del cuerpo) indican que era capaz de un considerable vuelo activo, contrario a algunas ideas iniciales de que las alas eran tan grandes que solo podían planear.

facts.statement: Like other pterosaurs, Pteranodon likely took off from a quadrupedal position.
facts.quote: Como otros pterosaurios, Pteranodon probablemente despegaba desde una posición cuadrúpeda.

facts.statement: Using its large limbs to leverage itself, it would have propelled itself into the air in a rapid jump.
facts.quote: Usando sus grandes miembros para apalancarse, se habría impulsado a sí mismo en el aire en un salto rápido.

facts.statement: Fossilized fish bones found in the stomach area and a fossilized fish bolus found between the jaws of specimen AMNH 5098 confirm that fish were a major part of the Pteranodon diet.
facts.quote: Se sabe que la dieta de Pteranodon incluía peces; huesos de peces fosilizados se han hallado en el área del estómago de un Pteranodon, y un bolo alimenticio fosilizado de peces se halló entre las mandíbulas de otro Pteranodon, el espécimen AMNH 5098.

facts.statement: Fragments of fish vertebrae and scales preserved near the torso of several specimens indicate that fish made up the majority of the Pteranodon diet, though it likely also ate invertebrates.
facts.quote: Varios otros ejemplares también preservan fragmentos de vértebras y escamas de pez cerca del torso, lo que indica que los peces constituían la mayoría de la dieta del Pteranodon (aunque también debió de haber capturado invertebrados).

facts.statement: In 1994, Bennett suggested that Pteranodon could dive by folding its wings back like a modern cormorant, noting that its head, neck, and shoulders were as robust as those of diving birds.
facts.quote: En 1994, Bennett notó que la cabeza, cuello y hombros de Pteranodon estaban tan fuertemente constituidos como las aves buceadoras, y sugirió que este animal podría sumergirse plegando sus alas hacia atrás como el moderno alcatraz.

facts.statement: Even a small female Pteranodon could likely reach a depth of at least 80 cm with its long beak and neck while floating, and may have dived from the air to reach greater depths like modern seabirds.
facts.quote: Incluso una pequeña hembra de Pteranodon pudo haber alcanzado una profundidad de al menos 80 cm. con su largo pico y cuello mientras flotaba en la superficie, y puede haber llegado a profundidades aún mayores zambulléndose al agua desde el aire como algunas aves marinas modernas.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Pteranodon caught fish by plunging its beak into water while gliding slowly, a hypothesis based on the assumption that the animal could not take off from the water surface.
facts.quote: Tradicionalmente, muchos investigadores han sugerido que Pteranodon pudo haber capturado peces sumergiendo sus picos en el agua en un lento planeo. Sin embargo, esta idea se basa en la suposición de que el animal no podía despegar desde la superficie del agua.

facts.statement: Pteranodon lived from the Coniacian to the Campanian stages, between 89.8 and 72.2 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Coniacian to Campanian (89.8 to 72.2 million years ago)

facts.statement: Pteranodon is classified within the class Reptilia.
